subject.title: Lives
subject.author: Derek Mahon
subject.text:
First time out
I was a torc of gold
And wept tears of the sun.
 
That was fun
But they buried me
In the earth two thousand years
 
Till a labourer
Turned me up with a pick
In eighteen fifty-four.
 
Once I was an oar
But stuck in the shore
To mark the place of a grave
 
When the lost ship
Sailed away. I thought
Of Ithaca, but soon decayed.
 
The time that I liked
Best was when
I was a bump of clay
 
In a Navaho rug,
Put there to mitigate
The too god-like
 
Perfection of that
Merely human artifact.
I served my maker well -
 
He lived long
To be struck down in
Denver by an electric shock
 
The night the lights
Went out in Europe
Never to shine again.
 
So many lives,
So many things to remember!
I was a stone in Tibet,
 
A tongue of bark
At the heart of Africa
Growing darker and darker . . . 
 
It all seems
A little unreal now,
Now that I am
 
An anthropologist
With my own
Credit card, dictaphone,
 
Army-surplus boots
And a whole boatload
Of photographic equipment.
 
I know too much
To be anything any more;
And if in the distant
 
Future someone
Thinks he has once been me
As I am today,
 
Let him revise
His insolent ontology
Or teach himself to pray.

title: A Dedication That Argues With the Dedicatee
standfirst: Derek Mahon gave this poem to his friend Seamus Heaney in 1972, the same year Heaney began digging up bog bodies and calling them ancestors — and used the dedication to quietly disagree with him.

sections.heading: A Gift With a Barb Folded Into It
sections.body:
The dedication most readers never see, because anthologies rarely print it, reads simply "for Seamus Heaney." Mahon and Heaney had known each other since the early 1960s, two of the Belfast poets who came up around Philip Hobsbaum's workshop, and by 1972 Heaney was becoming the most visible poet either of them knew personally. A dedication like that usually reads as a nod, or a debt repaid. This one reads more like a rejoinder.

"Lives" runs its speaker through a chain of reincarnations — a torc of gold, a grave-marker, a bump of clay, a stone, a strip of bark — before landing in the present day as a jobbing anthropologist "with my own / Credit card, dictaphone, / Army-surplus boots." The poem's last instruction, aimed past its own edge at whoever comes next, is to "revise / [their] insolent ontology / Or teach [themselves] to pray." A commentary on the poem's classical sources notes that this needling is deliberate: Mahon is [mocking his friend's](https://university.open.ac.uk/arts/research/greek-plays/poems-classical-referents/lives) own preoccupation with genealogy, dressed up as a poem about someone else's lives.

sections.heading: The Same Year, a Different Kind of Digging
sections.body:
1972 was also the year Heaney published *Wintering Out*, the collection that opened his run of bog poems with "The Tollund Man." Heaney had been reading P. V. Glob's study of Iron Age bodies preserved whole in Jutland's peat, and he found in them something like ancestors — a way to make sense of ritual killing in Northern Ireland's present by way of ritual killing in its bogs' deep past. He had already rehearsed the move three years earlier, closing *Door into the Dark* with "Bogland." For Heaney, digging something old out of the ground was a route to kinship: you found a body in the peat and it told you something true about where you were from.

Mahon's poem, written the same year, runs an almost identical operation — object after object, buried, dug up, reused — and refuses that payoff. His speaker does not arrive at continuity. It arrives exhausted: "I know too much / To be anything any more." Where Heaney's bog poems ask a reader to recognise a stranger as one of their own, Mahon's poem warns against exactly that recognition.

sections.heading: A Torc, an Oar, a Bump of Clay
sections.body:
The poem's first life is a torc of gold, buried two thousand years and dug up by a labourer "with a pick / In eighteen fifty-four" — a find date that echoes an anecdote Seán O'Faoláin told in *The Irish* (1947), his Penguin survey of national character, which Mahon is quietly borrowing and undercutting in the same breath.

The second life is an oar "stuck in the shore / To mark the place of a grave" when "the lost ship / Sailed away." That is Elpenor: the crewman in Book 12 of Homer's *Odyssey* who falls to his death on Circe's island, is left unburied in the rush to leave, and gets nothing more than an oar planted over him when the ship finally returns. Mahon liked the image enough to reuse it years later in another poem, "Light Music."

Then a "bump of clay," deliberately worked into a Navajo rug "to mitigate / The too god-like / Perfection of that / Merely human artifact" — an imperfection built in on purpose, by someone else's convention. The object becomes a stone in Tibet next, then a strip of bark "at the heart of Africa." It accumulates a geography with no say in any of it, borrowed and discarded by every culture that finds a use for it.

sections.heading: An Anthropologist Arrives, Credentialed and Late
sections.body:
For most of the poem, the thing speaking has been dug up, worn, buried, woven in. In the final turn it stops being excavated and starts excavating — it becomes, of all things, an anthropologist, kitted out in the gear of the professionalised present:

> An anthropologist
> With my own
> Credit card, dictaphone,
>
> Army-surplus boots
> And a whole boatload
> Of photographic equipment.

Having been so many things, it can no longer be any one of them without irony: "I know too much / To be anything any more." The poem's last three lines then turn outward, warning whoever might one day believe they were once this speaker to "revise / [their] insolent ontology / Or teach [themselves] to pray." Insolent ontology is the phrase people keep quoting back, and for good reason — it names, in two words, the specific presumption of digging something up and deciding it is yours by right of discovery. Mahon's dedication makes the target harder to miss.

sections.heading: Belfast Shipyard, Derry Farm
sections.body:
The joke sits on top of two very different childhoods. Mahon was born in Belfast in 1941, the only child of working-class Protestant parents; his father and grandfather both worked at the Harland & Wolff shipyard, his mother at a flax mill. Heaney was born two years earlier at Mossbawn farm near Castledawson, County Derry, the eldest of nine children of a cattle-dealing farmer and a mother from a linen-mill family, and was sent to a Catholic boarding school in Derry before Queen's University Belfast. Two different pasts to dig up, and — this poem suggests — two different instincts about what digging one up is allowed to prove.

They met through Philip Hobsbaum's Belfast Group in the early 1960s, though Mahon's own attendance was thin: he was mostly living abroad while the group ran and, by his own account, [went once](https://humag.co/features/the-belfast-group?edition=4). What he remembered clearly was the credibility Hobsbaum lent them simply by taking the work seriously — "he's actually taking us seriously," as Mahon put it. Hobsbaum, for his part, reportedly found Mahon's poems too elegant next to the rawer material he favoured, an early skirmish in the same argument "Lives" is still having with Heaney a decade later: control against excavation, wit against earnestness about the ground.
